paper_context.research_question: How can a fully automatic, cross-lingual name tagging and linking framework be developed for 282 Wikipedia languages, capable of identifying, typing, and linking name mentions to an English Knowledge Base, without manual annotations or native speaker knowledge?
main_claims: A fully automatic cross-lingual name tagging and linking framework has been developed for 282 Wikipedia languages.
The framework identifies name mentions, assigns coarse-grained or fine-grained types, and links them to an English Knowledge Base.

This is achieved through novel KB mining methods including cross-lingual entity transfer for silver-standard annotations, self-training for refinement, cross-lingual topic transfer for customization, Wikipedia markup-derived morphology features, and word translation mining from cross-lingual links.
The framework yields promising name tagging and linking results on Wikipedia data for 282 languages.
Results on non-Wikipedia data (news articles and discussion forum posts) are comparable to supervised models trained from manually annotated documents.
All developed data sets, resources, and systems for 282 languages will be made publicly available as a new benchmark.
expected_evaluation_dimensions: Performance (F-score, accuracy) of name tagging and linking across 282 languages on Wikipedia data.
Performance (F-score) of name tagging on non-Wikipedia data compared to state-of-the-art language-independent and supervised models.
Impact of specific methodological components, such as morphology analysis and self-training, on performance.
Scalability and generalizability of the framework to a large number of diverse languages, including low-resource, morphologically rich, and non-Latin script languages.
Utility and quality of the released 'silver-standard' annotations, morphology analyzers, and end-to-end systems as a benchmark.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Wikipedia's crowd-sourced markups (anchor links, cross-lingual links) and KB properties provide a sufficiently reliable and consistent source of 'natural annotations' for name tagging and linking across diverse languages.
supporting_evidence: Wikipedia is a massively multi-lingual resource that currently hosts 295 languages and contains naturally annotated markups 1 and rich informational structures through crowd-sourcing...

We start by assigning an entity type or “other” to each English Wikipedia entry. We utilize Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) corpus (Banarescu et al., 2013) where each entity name mention is manually labeled as one of 139 types and linked to Wikipedia if it’s linkable.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If Wikipedia markups are inconsistent or noisy for certain languages or entity types, the 'silver-standard' annotations and subsequent model training could be compromised, affecting performance and generalizability.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The entity types and linking annotations derived from the English AMR corpus and YAGO type hierarchy are universally applicable and meaningful across all 282 target languages.
supporting_evidence: We exploit the English Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) corpus (Banarescu et al., 2013) which includes both name tagging and linking annotations for fine-grained entity types to train an automatic classifier. We also map each AMR type to YAGO type hierarchy. Therefore, the generated typing schema has multiple levels of granularity.
For each pair of AMR entity type ta and YAGO entity type ty, we compute the Pointwise Mutual Information (Church and Hanks, 1990) of mapping ta to ty across all mentions in the AMR corpus.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Cultural or linguistic differences might mean that entity types or their granularity in English do not perfectly align with how entities are perceived or categorized in other languages, leading to misclassifications or reduced utility.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The 'silver-standard' annotations, despite being 'incomplete and inconsistent' initially, can be sufficiently refined through self-training and topic selection to produce high-quality training data.
supporting_evidence: However, such initial annotations are too incomplete and inconsistent. Previous work used name string match to propagate labels. In contrast, we apply self-training to label other mentions without links in Wikipedia articles even if they have different surface forms from the linked mentions (Section 2.3).
The name annotations acquired from the above procedure are far from complete to compete with manually labeled gold-standard data. ... We apply self-training to propagate and refine the labels.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If the initial noise in the 'silver-standard' is too high, or if the self-training process propagates errors, the quality of the refined annotations and the trained models could be negatively impacted.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The consistency of Wikipedia titles' style and format across languages allows for effective mining of word translation pairs using GIZA++.
supporting_evidence: Based on the observation that Wikipedia titles within any language tend to follow a consistent style and format, we propose an effective method to derive word translation pairs from these titles based on automatic alignment (Section 3.2).
Fortunately, these cross-lingual title pairs, generated through crowd-sourcing, generally follow a consistent style and format in each language.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If title styles are not consistently aligned, or if GIZA++ struggles with the specific characteristics of Wikipedia titles, the quality of word translation pairs could be low, hindering cross-lingual linking.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Performance on Wikipedia data using 'silver-standard' annotations, while not directly comparable to gold-standard, is a valid indicator of the framework's predictability and internal consistency.
supporting_evidence: Also note that since we don’t have perfect annotations on Wikipedia data for any language, these results can be used to estimate how predictable our “silver-standard” data is, but they are not directly comparable to traditional name tagging results measured against gold-standard data annotated by human.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Reviewers might misinterpret these results as absolute performance, or question their utility if the 'predictability' of silver-standard data does not correlate well with real-world performance on gold-standard data.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The 'commonness' and 'topical relatedness' criteria for training data selection effectively prioritize 'high-quality annotated sentences' for rapid system training in emergent settings.
supporting_evidence: Therefore we develop the following effective methods to rank and select high-quality annotated sentences.
Commonness: we prefer sentences that include common entities appearing frequently in Wikipedia.

Topical Relatedness: Various criteria should be adopted for different scenarios. Using an emergent disaster setting as a use case, we prefer sentences that include entities related to disaster related topics.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: The selected sentences might not be representative of the broader data distribution or might introduce biases, potentially limiting the generalizability or robustness of the rapidly trained system.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript presents a logically structured argument for a fully automatic, cross-lingual name tagging and linking framework spanning 282 Wikipedia languages. The core argument flows from identifying a critical need (breaking language barriers in crisis information) to leveraging a unique resource (Wikipedia's multilingual structure and KB properties), detailing novel methodological components, evaluating their performance, and concluding with the release of a significant benchmark. The paper's strength lies in its modular approach to address the challenges of large-scale, low-resource NLP, with each section building upon the previous one. However, the reliance on 'silver-standard' annotations for the primary evaluation introduces a critical caveat to the interpretation of performance claims, which the paper transparently acknowledges but does not fully resolve in terms of absolute quality. The transition from Wikipedia-internal evaluation to external, gold-standard comparison is a crucial point of continuity, though the performance gap remains a logical tension.
logical_argument_graph: Problem Statement (Section 1): Language barriers hinder information extraction in crises, necessitating cross-lingual solutions.
Resource Identification (Section 1): Wikipedia offers a massively multilingual, naturally annotated resource (295 languages, anchor links, cross-lingual links, KB properties).
Goal (Section 1): Develop a fully automatic, cross-lingual name tagging and linking framework for 282 Wikipedia languages, linking to an English KB without manual annotations.
Methodology - Name Tagging (Section 2):
- Annotation Generation (Section 2.2): Classify English KB pages using AMR/YAGO types and KB properties (C8, C7), then propagate to other languages via cross-lingual links (Assumption A2).
- Self-Training (Section 2.3): Refine initial incomplete/inconsistent 'silver-standard' annotations using Bi-LSTM-CRF and NPMI-based seed selection (Assumption A3).
- Training Data Selection (Section 2.4): For populous languages, select high-quality sentences based on 'commonness' and 'topical relatedness' for rapid training (Assumption A6).
- KB Derived Features (Section 2.5): Automatically learn morphology features (stems, affixes) from Wikipedia markups for morphologically rich languages.
Methodology - Cross-lingual Entity Linking (Section 3):
- Name Translation (Section 3.2): Mine word translation pairs from cross-lingual Wikipedia title pairs using GIZA++ (Assumption A4).
- Entity Linking (Section 3.3): Apply unsupervised collective inference to link translated English mentions to an English KB using knowledge networks and similarity measures.

Evaluation - Internal (Section 4.1): Assess name tagging and linking performance on Wikipedia data using 'silver-standard' annotations for 282 languages (C4). Acknowledge non-comparability to gold-standard (Assumption A5).

Evaluation - External (Section 4.2): Compare name tagging performance on non-Wikipedia (news/forum) gold-standard data for 9 languages against state-of-the-art language-independent and supervised models (C5, C11). Demonstrate impact of morphology features (C9).
Evaluation - Component Impact (Section 4.3): Quantify the significant F-score gains from self-training (C10).

Conclusion & Impact (Section 6): The framework is effective, applied to the largest number of languages (C12), and all resources will be publicly released as a new benchmark (C6). Future work includes cross-lingual knowledge transfer and extending to other IE tasks.

alternative_interpretations: The 'promising' results on Wikipedia data might primarily reflect the internal consistency of the 'silver-standard' generation process rather than absolute real-world performance, especially for languages with sparse data or complex linguistic features.

The performance drop for certain language groups (e.g., non-Latin scripts, no word spacing) could indicate fundamental limitations of the Wikipedia markup-driven approach for these languages, rather than just data sparsity or imbalance.

The 'fully automatic' claim, while technically true, might imply a level of performance parity with supervised methods that the reported F-score differences do not fully support, suggesting a trade-off rather than a direct replacement.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The sheer scale of 282 languages and the fully automatic, annotation-free approach for name tagging and linking to an English KB is a significant innovation. While the 'silver-standard' approach introduces validity concerns regarding absolute performance, the methodology itself represents a novel and ambitious attempt to overcome resource scarcity in extreme multilingual NLP. The challenge is not in the concept's validity, but in the practical realization of high-quality data and performance across such a diverse linguistic landscape.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If the 'silver-standard' annotations, despite initial noise, prove to be sufficiently high-quality and consistent across all 282 languages after refinement, the framework's utility would be maximized.

If the performance gap with supervised models on gold-standard data can be further narrowed through future enhancements (e.g., more sophisticated cross-lingual knowledge transfer or semi-supervised techniques) without reintroducing manual annotation, the framework would become a compelling alternative.

If the released datasets and systems are widely adopted and enable downstream applications in low-resource languages, demonstrating practical impact beyond reported metrics, the contribution would be validated.

If the English-derived entity typing schema is found to be robust and culturally appropriate for a significant majority of the 282 languages, or if mechanisms for language-specific type adaptation are developed, the framework's semantic richness would be enhanced.

novelty_lenses.rationale: The application of a fully automatic, annotation-free framework to 282 Wikipedia languages for name tagging and linking is a significant leap in scale and automation compared to prior work, which often focused on fewer languages or required some manual intervention. This addresses a critical resource bottleneck in multilingual NLP.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper presents an ambitious and innovative framework for fully automatic, cross-lingual name tagging and linking across 282 Wikipedia languages, explicitly designed to operate without manual annotations or native speaker knowledge. The methodology hinges on a series of clever Knowledge Base (KB) mining techniques, including the generation of 'silver-standard' annotations via cross-lingual entity transfer, iterative refinement through self-training, and the derivation of language-specific features like morphology from Wikipedia markups. While the framework demonstrates promising internal consistency on Wikipedia data and outperforms existing language-independent methods on external datasets, a critical audit reveals several methodological and robustness concerns. The reliance on 'silver-standard' annotations, despite self-training, introduces inherent noise and limits direct comparability to gold-standard evaluations. Performance significantly degrades for low-resource, non-Latin script, and non-space-delimited languages, indicating a lack of uniform robustness across the claimed 282 languages. Furthermore, the 'comparable' performance on non-Wikipedia data still shows a notable gap to supervised models, and this evaluation is limited to a small subset of languages. The universality of English-derived entity types across diverse cultures is also an unvalidated assumption. The planned release of resources is a significant strength for reproducibility, but the quality and generalizability of these 'silver-standard' derived assets warrant careful consideration.

concerns.title: Validity of 'Silver-Standard' Evaluation
concerns.description: The primary evaluation on Wikipedia data relies on 'silver-standard' annotations, which the paper transparently admits are 'not directly comparable to traditional name tagging results measured against gold-standard data'. While useful for internal consistency, this limits the ability to assess the absolute performance and true validity of the framework's output on its core dataset. The 'predictability' of silver-standard data does not equate to its accuracy or completeness.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript proposes a fully automatic, cross-lingual name tagging and linking framework designed for 282 Wikipedia languages. The core reasoning is that by leveraging the rich, crowd-sourced annotations and structured information within Wikipedia (anchor links, cross-lingual links, KB properties), it's possible to generate 'silver-standard' training data and derive language-specific features without any manual annotation or native speaker knowledge. This framework then identifies name mentions, assigns multi-grained types, and links them to an English Knowledge Base. Key methodological innovations include cross-lingual entity transfer for initial annotations, self-training for refinement, cross-lingual topic transfer for customization, Wikipedia markup-derived morphology features, and word translation mining from cross-lingual links. The paper demonstrates that this approach yields promising results on Wikipedia data and competitive performance on non-Wikipedia data compared to state-of-the-art language-independent methods, while acknowledging a gap to fully supervised models. A significant contribution is the planned public release of the generated datasets, resources, and systems for all 282 languages, establishing a new benchmark for large-scale, low-resource NLP.
logical_argument_graph: The problem of cross-lingual name tagging and linking is resource-intensive, especially for a massive number of languages (Section 1).
Wikipedia offers a massively multilingual resource with 'naturally annotated markups' and rich informational structures (Section 1).
Therefore, Wikipedia can be leveraged to develop a fully automatic, cross-lingual name tagging and linking framework for 282 languages without manual annotations (Claim C1, C2).

This is achieved through a series of novel KB mining methods: cross-lingual entity transfer for silver-standard annotations, self-training for refinement, cross-lingual topic transfer for customization, Wikipedia markup-derived morphology features, and word translation mining from cross-lingual links (Claim C3).

The framework's annotation generation process starts by classifying English Wikipedia pages into multi-level entity types using AMR and YAGO, leveraging KB properties as features, achieving high accuracy (Claim C7, C8, Section 2.2).
These English annotations are then propagated to other languages via cross-lingual links to create 'silver-standard' data (Section 2.2).
Self-training is applied to refine these initial, incomplete annotations, significantly improving performance (Claim C10, Section 2.3).
For morphologically rich languages, morphology features are automatically derived from Wikipedia anchor markups, contributing substantial F-score gains (Claim C9, Section 2.5).
Word translation pairs are mined from cross-lingual Wikipedia title pairs using GIZA++ to enable cross-lingual entity linking (Section 3.2).
The entity linking process uses an unsupervised collective inference approach, similar to prior work, based on translated name mentions and knowledge networks (Section 3.3).
The framework yields promising name tagging and linking results on Wikipedia data for 282 languages, though these are not directly comparable to gold-standard evaluations (Claim C4, Section 4.1).
On non-Wikipedia data, the framework's results are comparable to supervised models and outperform state-of-the-art language-independent methods (Claim C5, C11, Section 4.2).
The framework is applied to the largest number of languages (282) to date (Claim C12).
All developed data sets, resources, and systems for 282 languages will be made publicly available as a new benchmark (Claim C6, Section 6).
Therefore, the paper presents a simple yet effective framework for large-scale, fully automatic cross-lingual name tagging and linking, making a significant resource contribution (Section 6).

strengths.title: Effective Integration of KB Mining Techniques for Automatic Annotation
strengths.description: The paper refines existing paradigms of distant supervision and cross-lingual projection by integrating multiple KB mining methods to create 'silver-standard' annotations. This includes cross-lingual entity transfer from English AMR/YAGO, self-training for label refinement, and topic-based selection, which collectively enable a fully automatic pipeline for generating training data at scale. This systematic combination and application of known techniques to generate high-quality, large-scale training data without human intervention is a notable incremental contribution.
evidence: We achieve this goal by performing a series of new KB mining methods: generating “silver-standard” annotations by transferring annotations from English to other languages through crosslingual links and KB properties, refining annotations through self-training and topic selection...
We utilize Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) corpus (Banarescu et al., 2013) where each entity name mention is manually labeled as one of 139 types and linked to Wikipedia if it’s linkable.
We apply self-training to propagate and refine the labels.
Self-training provides significant improvement for both Wikipedia (6% absolute gain) and Non-Wikipedia test data (12% absolute gain).

strengths.title: Novel Derivation of Language-Specific Features from Wikipedia Markups
strengths.description: The method of automatically deriving morphology features (stems and affixes) directly from Wikipedia anchor markups for morphologically rich languages is an elegant and practical refinement of using Wikipedia as a resource. This approach bypasses the need for high-cost supervised or low-quality unsupervised morphological analysis, providing significant performance gains (e.g., 11.1% F-score for Turkish), and extends the utility of Wikipedia's inherent structure.

The morphology features contributed 11.1% and 7.1% absolute F-score gains to Turkish and Uzbek respectively.

Previous methods relied on either high-cost supervised learning (Roth et al., 2008; Mahmoudi et al., 2013; Ahlberg et al., 2015), or low-quality unsupervised learning (Gronroos et al., 2014; Ruokolainen et al., 2016).

concerns.title: Reliance on 'Silver-Standard' Data and Performance Gap
concerns.description: While the framework successfully generates 'silver-standard' annotations automatically, the inherent limitations of this data (acknowledged as 'incomplete and inconsistent' and 'not perfect') mean that the reported performance on Wikipedia data is not directly comparable to gold-standard evaluations. Furthermore, on non-Wikipedia data, despite outperforming language-independent methods, the framework still shows a noticeable performance gap (5.8% - 17.6% lower F-scores) compared to supervised models. This suggests that while the approach is highly scalable and automatic, there's an inherent trade-off in annotation quality and ultimate performance compared to human-curated data.

concerns.title: Varying Performance Across Language Characteristics
concerns.description: The paper notes significant performance drops for languages with fewer mentions, those without spaces between words (e.g., Chinese, Thai, Japanese), and non-Latin scripts (e.g., Dravidian group). While these are common challenges in multilingual NLP, the framework's 'fully automatic' claim implies a degree of robustness across all 282 languages. The observed performance variations suggest that the incremental methods, while generally effective, do not uniformly address the unique linguistic challenges posed by all language families, indicating areas where further refinement is needed.
evidence: Not surprisingly, name tagging performs better for languages with more mentions. The fscore is generally higher than 80% when there are more than 30K mentions, and it significantly drops when there are less than 250 mentions.

The languages with low name tagging performance can be categorized into three types: (1) the number of mentions is less than 2K... (2) there is no space between words, including Chinese, Thai and Japanese; (3) they are not written in latin script, such as the Dravidian group (Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam).
concerns.actionable_suggestion: The authors could discuss specific strategies or future work directions to explicitly address the challenges posed by languages with sparse data, non-segmenting scripts, or non-Latin scripts, rather than just noting the performance drop. This would enhance the incremental contribution by outlining paths for further generalization.

concerns.title: Generalizability of English-Derived Typing Schema
concerns.description: The framework relies on entity types and linking annotations derived from the English AMR corpus and YAGO hierarchy. While this provides a rich, multi-grained schema, there's an implicit assumption (A2) that these categories are universally applicable and culturally meaningful across all 282 diverse languages. Cultural or linguistic nuances might mean that certain entity types or their granularity in English do not perfectly align with how entities are perceived or categorized in other languages, potentially limiting the framework's utility or introducing biases for some languages.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript presents a highly ambitious and potentially disruptive framework for fully automatic, cross-lingual name tagging and linking across 282 Wikipedia languages. The core reasoning is to circumvent the traditional reliance on manual annotations and native speaker knowledge by systematically leveraging Wikipedia's inherent crowd-sourced structure and external Knowledge Base (KB) properties. This involves novel KB mining methods, including cross-lingual entity transfer to generate 'silver-standard' annotations, self-training to refine them, cross-lingual topic transfer for customization, derivation of language-specific morphology features from Wikipedia markups, and mining word translation pairs from cross-lingual links. The framework aims to identify, type (coarse-grained to fine-grained, linked to an English KB), and link name mentions. The evaluation demonstrates promising results on Wikipedia data and performance comparable to state-of-the-art language-independent methods (and somewhat lower than supervised models) on non-Wikipedia data. The ultimate goal is to release all developed datasets, resources, and systems for these 282 languages as a new benchmark, thereby democratizing access to NLP capabilities for a vast array of languages, including many low-resource ones.
logical_argument_graph: Problem: Existing cross-lingual name tagging and linking methods are resource-intensive, requiring manual annotations or native speaker knowledge, limiting scalability to hundreds of diverse languages.
Proposed Solution: Develop a fully automatic framework that leverages Wikipedia's multi-lingual structure and KB properties as 'natural annotations' and features.

Mechanism 1 (Annotation Generation): Classify English Wikipedia entries into entity types (using AMR/YAGO) and propagate these labels to other languages via cross-lingual links, creating 'silver-standard' annotations.
Mechanism 2 (Annotation Refinement): Apply self-training to propagate and refine these initial, incomplete, and inconsistent 'silver-standard' labels to unlabeled mentions.

Mechanism 3 (Feature Engineering): Derive language-specific morphology features from Wikipedia markups (anchor links) and mine word translation pairs from cross-lingual Wikipedia titles using alignment techniques (GIZA++).
Mechanism 4 (Training Data Selection): Implement commonness and topical relatedness criteria to select high-quality annotated sentences for rapid system training, especially for emergent settings.

Mechanism 5 (Entity Linking): Translate identified names to English using mined translations, then apply unsupervised collective inference to link them to an English KB (DBpedia) based on salience, similarity, and coherence.
Evaluation 1 (Internal Consistency): Assess name tagging and linking performance on Wikipedia data using the generated 'silver-standard' annotations across 282 languages.

Evaluation 2 (External Comparability): Evaluate name tagging performance on non-Wikipedia data (news, forums) for a subset of languages, comparing against state-of-the-art language-independent and supervised models.
Impact Assessment: Quantify the contribution of key components like morphology features and self-training.
Conclusion: The framework yields promising results, outperforms previous language-independent methods, and is comparable to supervised models on non-Wikipedia data (with a gap).

Contribution: Release of the largest-scale multilingual name tagging and linking framework, including 'silver-standard' annotations, morphology analyzers, and end-to-end systems for 282 languages as a new benchmark.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript presents a framework for fully automatic, cross-lingual name tagging and linking across 282 Wikipedia languages, aiming to circumvent the need for manual annotations or native speaker knowledge. The core reasoning is that Wikipedia's extensive multilingual structure and Knowledge Base properties can be leveraged to generate 'silver-standard' annotations and derive language-specific features. The paper details several novel KB mining methods, including cross-lingual entity transfer, self-training for refinement, Wikipedia markup-derived morphology features, and word translation mining. While the claims of full automation, broad language coverage, and the specific methodological innovations are well-supported by the described system design and quantified component impacts, the claims regarding overall performance require more nuanced interpretation. The 'promising' results on Wikipedia data are explicitly noted as not directly comparable to gold-standard evaluations and show significant variability across languages, particularly for low-resource or typologically challenging ones. Similarly, the 'comparable' performance on non-Wikipedia data, while outperforming language-independent baselines, still presents a notable performance gap (5.8% - 17.6% lower F-scores) compared to supervised models. The commitment to release all resources as a new benchmark is a significant strength, but the inherent limitations of the 'silver-standard' data will influence its utility.
logical_argument_graph: Problem: Language barriers hinder information extraction in crises, requiring cross-lingual name tagging and linking (NTL) for many languages.
Challenge: Traditional NTL requires extensive manual annotations and native speaker knowledge, which is scarce for hundreds of languages.
Proposed Solution: Develop a fully automatic, cross-lingual NTL framework for 282 Wikipedia languages, leveraging Wikipedia's crowd-sourced data and KB properties.
Methodology (Novel KB Mining):
- Generate 'silver-standard' annotations via cross-lingual entity transfer from English AMR/YAGO types (C3, C7, C8).
- Refine annotations using self-training (C3, C10).
- Customize annotations via cross-lingual topic transfer (C3).
- Derive language-specific morphology features from Wikipedia markups (C3, C9).
- Mine word translation pairs from cross-lingual links (C3).
Framework Capabilities: Identifies name mentions, assigns multi-grained types, and links to an English KB (C2).
Evaluation (Wikipedia Data): Demonstrates 'promising' name tagging and linking results on Wikipedia data for 282 languages, with caveats regarding comparability and performance variations (C4).
Evaluation (Non-Wikipedia Data): Achieves 'comparable' performance to supervised models and outperforms state-of-the-art language-independent methods on external datasets (C5, C11).
Contribution: The framework is applied to the largest number of languages (C12) and all developed datasets, resources, and systems will be publicly released as a new benchmark (C6).

All the data sets, resources and systems for 282 languages will be made publicly available as a new benchmark.

Content: Starting with February 2025, ARR reviewers are asked to provide three scores: soundness, excitement, and overall recommendation. I3 The soundness scores must be justified by the text of the review . If you give a low Soundness score without finding any major faults, this means that your review is not a faithful explanation of your recommendation, and you need to revise it. One possible reason for low soundness scores without sufficient justification could be reliance on some unconscious bias or heuristic, like the ones listed in the previous section. Likewise, low reproducibility scores should be justified. Sometimes you may find the work sound, but not something that is interesting for you personally. Such preferences are more subjective and should be reflected in a separate excitement score, which is orthogonal to the assessment of the soundness of the paper. Excitement scores reflect our personal taste, and so do not necessarily come with explicit reasons. The Overall assessment score is an explicit recommendation for the outcome of this paper, if it were committed to an *ACL venue. This is a composite score reflecting your assessment of soundness, excitement, and also other factors like novelty and impact. All papers recommended for Findings and main conferences are expected to be sufficiently sound and reproducible, but you may consider a paper worthy of the main conference even if you personally are not excited about it.

Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 5. Check that your scores reflect the review I3
Codes: I3
Applies To: meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: Starting with February 2025, ARR reviewers are asked to provide three scores: soundness, excitement, and overall recommendation. I3 The soundness scores must be justified by the text of the review . If you give a low Soundness score without finding any major faults, this means that your review is not a faithful explanation of your recommendation, and you need to revise it. One possible reason for low soundness scores without sufficient justification could be reliance on some unconscious bias or heuristic, like the ones listed in the previous section. Likewise, low reproducibility scores should be justified. Sometimes you may find the work sound, but not something that is interesting for you personally. Such preferences are more subjective and should be reflected in a separate excitement score, which is orthogonal to the assessment of the soundness of the paper. Excitement scores reflect our personal taste, and so do not necessarily come with explicit reasons. The Overall assessment score is an explicit recommendation for the outcome of this paper, if it were committed to an *ACL venue. This is a composite score reflecting your assessment of soundness, excitement, and also other factors like novelty and impact. All papers recommended for Findings and main conferences are expected to be sufficiently sound and reproducible, but you may consider a paper worthy of the main conference even if you personally are not excited about it.

Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation.
